# Why orders 0 and 1 are binned in physical time {#sec-histogram-binning}

`readout.py` computes a 1 ns histogram two different ways at once: the
$\ge2$-scattering component is Fourier-inverted from a finite frequency
grid (@sec-charge), while orders 0 and 1 are integrated directly in
physical time and then, if requested, convolved with the Gaussian
instrument response through a difference of normal CDFs. The code says so
in one line of its own diagnostics,
`"low_orders": "0 and 1 integrated in physical time; only >=2 Fourier-inverted"`,
but not why. This chapter answers that: orders 0 and 1 are singular
functions of time, and a finite-bandwidth frequency-domain bin filter is
the wrong tool for a singular function, however well it works for the
smooth $\ge2$ remainder. The bin value for a singular order still has to
be obtained by pairing the detector's window function with the transport
solution — that part of the reasoning is completely general — it is only
the *route* to that pairing that has to change.

## The general detector-bin functional {#sec-general-bin}

For a fixed observation point, the measured quantity in a bin
$[t_1,t_2]$ is the time integral of the (possibly instrument-smeared)
response $K(t)$:
$$
N_{[t_1,t_2]}=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}(h_d*K)(t)\,\mathrm dt,
$$
where $h_d$ is a normalized instrument response ($h_d=\delta$ when there is
no smearing). Writing this with the Fourier transform
$\tilde K(\omega)=\int\mathrm dt\,e^{i\omega t}K(t)$ and its inverse gives
$$
N_{[t_1,t_2]}=\int\frac{\mathrm d\omega}{2\pi}\,
W_{12}(\omega)\,H_d(\omega)\,\tilde K(\omega),
\qquad
W_{12}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-i\omega t_1}-e^{-i\omega t_2}}{i\omega},
$$
with $W_{12}(0)=t_2-t_1$ and $H_d(\omega)=\int\mathrm du\,e^{i\omega u}h_d(u)$
(for a Gaussian of width $\sigma$, $H_d(\omega)=e^{-\omega^2\sigma^2/2}$).
This is exactly the `sinc`-and-phase kernel used in `frequency_weights` /
`inverse_bins`: $W_{12}$ multiplied by the trapezoidal frequency weights
and the Gaussian factor, real-part-summed over the frequency grid, is the
`kernel` array built in `inverse_bins`.

This identity holds for **every** order — 0, 1, and $\ge2$ alike — because
it says nothing about $K$ beyond having a Fourier transform. What differs
between orders is not this formula; it is whether evaluating the right-hand
side on a truncated, evenly spaced frequency grid is a good approximation.

## Orders 0 and 1 are singular in time {#sec-singular-orders}

The ballistic order is a literal Dirac delta at the light front,
$$
K^{(0)}(t)=N_0\,\delta(t-\tau_0),\qquad
N_0=\frac{e^{-\mu_tr}}{4\pi r^2}\ \text{(isotropic source; @sec-setup)}.
$$
A delta function has $|\tilde K^{(0)}(\omega)|=N_0$ for **every**
$\omega$ — no decay at all. Sampling that on any finite grid and summing a
truncated inverse transform does not converge to a delta as the number of
retained frequencies grows in the way used for a smooth function; it
converges to a band-limited approximation of one, i.e. a ripple of width
$\sim1/\omega_{\max}$ centered on $\tau_0$, not a spike. There is no value
of $\omega_{\max}$ short of "large enough that the ripple is narrower than
the bin" that makes this route accurate, and for $\sigma=0$ no finite
$\omega_{\max}$ ever removes the ripple entirely.

Order 1 is not a delta, but it is not smooth either. In the isotropic
check of @sec-coordinate-first,
$$
K^{(1)}(r,t)=\frac{\mu_s}{4\pi rt}e^{-\mu_tvt}\ln\frac{vt+r}{vt-r},
\qquad t>r/v,
$$
which diverges logarithmically as $t\to(r/v)^+$ — this is exactly the
`+inf` that `single_scattering_rate` returns at `S == r` for an isotropic
flash. The general directed formula of @sec-coordinate-first has the same
character: its denominator $b\,(s-r\nu)$ can approach zero near the front,
producing a sharp near-front rise rather than a genuine infinity, depending
on geometry. Either way, a sharp, narrowly localized feature in time is,
by the uncertainty relation between the two domains, a **slowly decaying**
feature in frequency: $\tilde K^{(1)}(\omega)$ (what `single_spectrum`
computes) is perfectly finite and smooth in $\omega$, but it does not fall
off fast enough for a frequency grid sized for the $\ge2$ remainder to
represent its inverse transform accurately near the front.

The $\ge2$-scattering remainder does not have this problem. Physically,
each additional scattering convolves the path-length distribution with
another single-scatter kernel; summing infinitely many scattering orders
(@sec-orders) produces a response that turns on smoothly at the front
rather than jumping or diverging there — there is no single sharp feature
left to resolve. That is precisely why @sec-charge could afford to build
its spectrum on a modest, evenly spaced grid (241 nodes to 1.2 rad/ns) and
invert it with a plain frequency sum, at the cost of the periodic-image
caveat already noted there — a cost worth paying for a smooth function, and
not one that a sharp or infinite time-domain feature would tolerate.

## The fix: fold the window onto the closed form, not onto a truncated spectrum {#sec-fold}

@sec-general-bin's identity is still exactly what is being evaluated for
orders 0 and 1 — only the method of evaluating it changes. Instead of
approximating $\tilde K(\omega)$ on a grid and summing, the code uses the
fact that $K^{(0)}$ and $K^{(1)}$ have **known closed forms in time**, and
carries out the $\omega$-integral of @sec-general-bin analytically or by
adaptive quadrature directly on those closed forms:

- For order 0, $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}h_d*K^{(0)}\,\mathrm dt$ reduces to a single
  evaluation: the bin containing $\tau_0$ when $\sigma=0$ (a `searchsorted`
  lookup in `readout.py`), or
  $N_0\bigl[\Phi((t_2-\tau_0)/\sigma)-\Phi((t_1-\tau_0)/\sigma)\bigr]$ with
  the normal CDF $\Phi$ when $\sigma>0$ — exact, with no frequency grid
  involved at all.
- For order 1, `single_bins` integrates $K^{(1)}(t)$ (or its Gaussian
  convolution, via the same CDF-difference trick applied under the
  integral) over $[t_1,t_2]$ with adaptive quadrature (`scipy.integrate.quad`
  / `quad_vec`), which concentrates evaluation points near the light front
  on its own, exactly where the smooth trapezoidal frequency grid would
  need an unreasonably high $\omega_{\max}$ to do the same job indirectly.

Both routes compute the **same** number that @sec-general-bin defines, to
the requested tolerance; `test_single_raw_bins_are_causal_and_integrate_charge`
checks the two against each other by comparing the summed bins to
`single_spectrum`'s own $\omega=0$ value. The difference is only that the
time-domain route pays its accuracy cost where the singularity actually is,
while the frequency-domain route pays an accuracy cost everywhere in
$\omega$ whether or not the underlying function needs it there.

This is the "smart" scheme: fold the detector's own window/instrument
kernel directly onto the exact, singular pieces, and reserve the numerically
built, truncated-frequency-grid inversion for the piece that is smooth
enough for a fixed grid to represent well. Both are instances of the one
identity in @sec-general-bin; neither is a different physical model, and
neither privileges one order over another — the split follows the
regularity of $K$, not the collision count as such.

## What this does not claim {#sec-histogram-caveats}

The $\ge2$ remainder is smooth **relative to the sharpness of orders 0 and
1**, not perfectly band-limited; @sec-charge's periodic-image caveat still
applies to it, and its own convergence in $L,J,k,\omega$ still needs
checking case by case (@sec-checks). Splitting the computation this way
does not by itself bound the error of the $\ge2$ part, and it says nothing
about a finite OM's angular acceptance, which is not modeled yet
(@sec-setup). It only removes a specific, avoidable source of error — an
under-resolved frequency grid applied to functions that were never smooth
enough for it in the first place.
